records.old: which is larger and more complex than the full cone net from Lesson 1

records.old: two concentric annular sectors plus two circles — which is visibly larger and more complex than the rectangular net of a cylinder of equal height

records.old: After marking, ask: 'Omondi, which bucket — cylinder or sphere — needs more sheet metal for 10 litres? What does that tell the shopkeeper?' [WAIT 15 seconds]. Ensure the class hears that the sphere, for a given volume, has the minimum possible surface area — a key insight for the driving question.
records.new: Before Example 2, spend 3 minutes recalling the cylinder from earlier grades: roll a sheet of paper into an open cylinder and ask 'What shape is the curved part when unrolled? What are its sides?' (a rectangle 2πr by h), so the open bucket needs 2πrh + πr². After marking, give the answers: tank 4π(1.5)² ≈ 28.3 m²; open bucket 2π(10.6)(28.4) + π(10.6)² ≈ 2,244 cm². Do not yet say which shape is best: the fair comparison with a sphere of the same 10-litre volume is made in Model Building.
records.why: Gives the missing cylinder recall and the expected answers (recomputed: 2π(10.6)(28.4)=1,891.5; π(10.6)²=353.0; total 2,244.5). It also removes the claim that 'the sphere has the minimum surface area for a given volume' being shown by comparing it with an open bucket: a closed 10-litre sphere is about 2,245 cm², almost equal to the open bucket, so the lesson would have shown the opposite of what the teacher was told to say.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, Sphere and Cylinder; the isoperimetric property of the sphere (least surface area for a given volume among closed solids)
records.group_headline: The cylinder bucket is used in Lessons 3, 6 and 8 but its surface area was never taught; Lesson 3 now has a short cylinder recall and the Lesson 1 model page has a place for it

records.old: Then, as a group challenge, they calculate surface areas for all four 'buckets' in the phenomenon: Cylinder (open bucket), Open Cone (πrl + πr², using the Lesson 8 Bucket Data Sheet dimensions r = 13.4 cm, h = 52.9 cm), Sphere (today; a hypothetical closed fourth shape, not one of the shop's three open buckets; its radius, 13.4 cm, only coincidentally equals the cone's base radius), and leave the Frustum row blank with the label 'Coming in Lesson 5.' Groups compare their four values and write a ranked list: 'From least to most sheet metal: ___.' Finally, each learner writes a one-sentence 'model statement': 'For a fixed volume of 10 litres, the [shape] requires the least sheet metal because ___.' This statement will be revised as more evidence is gathered.
records.new: Then, as a group challenge, they compare the sphere with the buckets of the phenomenon. They use the sphere that holds 10 litres (a hypothetical closed fourth shape, not one of the shop's three buckets): radius ≈ 13.4 cm and surface area ≈ 2,245 cm². They set it beside the open cylindrical bucket from Example 2 (≈ 2,244 cm²) and the open conical bucket from the Lesson 1 extension (≈ 2,298 cm², curved surface only), and leave the Frustum row blank with the label 'Coming in Lesson 5.' Because the sphere has no opening, they also find the cylinder with a lid (≈ 2,597 cm²) and write a ranked list: 'From least to most sheet metal, for closed shapes of 10 litres: ___.' Finally, each learner writes a one-sentence 'model statement': 'For a fixed volume of 10 litres, the sphere needs the least sheet metal of any closed shape because ___.' This statement will be revised as more evidence is gathered.
records.why: Recomputed: sphere with V = 10,000 cm³ has r = (3 × 10,000 / 4π)^(1/3) = 13.37 cm and SA = 4πr² = 2,245 cm² (2,256 if r is rounded to 13.4 cm). The open cylinder is 2,244 cm², so a closed sphere is almost equal to an OPEN bucket; with a lid the cylinder is 2,597 cm², and the sphere is clearly the smallest closed shape. The old text also used cone formula πrl + πr² for an open cone and sent learners to a 'Lesson 8 data sheet' that they had not yet seen, and asked groups to compute four buckets in the last minutes of an 80-minute lesson.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, Sphere; isoperimetric inequality (sphere has least surface area for given volume)
records.group_headline: Lesson 3 ranked a closed sphere against OPEN buckets (and called the cone 'πrl + πr²'), so the sphere looked no better than the cylinder; now it compares fairly, with the correct 10-litre sphere values

records.old: After 4 minutes: 'Now, in your groups, use the 10-litre volume to find the radius of a sphere holding 10 litres.' [V = (4/3)πr³ → r ≈ 13.4 cm]. Write the setup on the board — do NOT solve it for them. Cold-call one group: 'Kisumu group — what radius did you get?' [WAIT 15 seconds]. Then: 'Now compute SA = 4πr² for that radius and add it to your comparison table.' Close by asking: 'Based on what we know so far — three of the four shapes — is the shopkeeper's claim about the frustum looking plausible or unlikely? Turn and tell your partner in one sentence.'
records.new: After 4 minutes: 'Now find the radius of a sphere that holds 10 litres.' Write the setup on the board: V = (4/3)πr³, so r³ = 3 × 10 000 ÷ 4π ≈ 2,387 and r ≈ 13.4 cm (13.37 more exactly). Do the cube root with the class (calculator or a table of cubes): it is not the focus of the lesson. Then: 'Compute SA = 4πr² and add it to your table.' (Expected ≈ 2,245 cm².) Ask: 'The sphere has no hole at the top. Is it fair to compare it with an open bucket?' Lead learners to add a lid to the cylinder (≈ 2,597 cm²) and see that the sphere is then the smallest. Close by asking: 'Based on what we know so far, is the shopkeeper's claim about the frustum looking plausible or unlikely? Turn and tell your partner in one sentence.'
records.why: Matches the corrected model-building task and gives the teacher the setup and expected value.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, Sphere

records.old: slant height of longer triangular faces = 12 cm, slant height of shorter triangular faces = 12.6 cm
records.new: slant height of the two faces on the 8 cm edges = 12 cm, slant height of the two faces on the 6 cm edges ≈ 12.3 cm
records.why: In a rectangular pyramid the slant heights are √(h² + 3²) and √(h² + 4²), so they differ by 4² − 3² = 7 in squared value. With 12 cm for the first, the second is √(144 + 7) = √151 = 12.29 cm, not 12.6 cm (12.6 would not fit the same apex, so the net would not close).
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, Pyramid (slant height of a right rectangular pyramid)
records.group_headline: The two slant heights given for the 8 × 6 rectangular pyramid could not belong to one pyramid (the net would not close); corrected to 12 cm and about 12.3 cm, with the expected total areas added

records.old: (b) Numerical answer of 360 cm² for the square pyramid verification. (c) In the application problem, learners correctly use slant height (not vertical height) and correctly handle the 'open base' variation.
records.new: (b) Numerical answers: 360 cm² for the square pyramid; 48 + 8(12) + 6(12.3) ≈ 217.8 cm² for the rectangular pyramid. (c) In the application problem, learners correctly use slant height (not vertical height) and correctly handle the 'open base' variation. Expected: 4 × ½ × 15 × 20 = 600 cm² per box; 200 boxes = 120 000 cm²; with 10% wastage 132 000 cm²; one A0 sheet is about 84.1 × 118.9 ≈ 10 000 cm², so 13.2, i.e. 14 sheets (more in practice because nets do not tile perfectly).
records.why: Adds expected answers for the rectangular pyramid and the A0-sheet problem (recomputed: 84.1 × 118.9 = 9,999.5; 132,000 / 9,999.5 = 13.2).

records.why: The old text said the hemisphere with the same volume as the 10-litre buckets has radius about 13.4 cm; that is the radius of a SPHERE of 10 litres. Hemisphere: r³ = 3 × 10,000 / 2π = 4,775, so r = 16.84 cm; 2π(16.84)² = 1,782 cm². Checked twice with a calculator.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, Hemisphere (volume ⅔πr³, curved area 2πr²)

records.old: R (top radius of frustum, the larger end), r (base radius of frustum, the smaller end)
records.new: R (radius of the larger end of the frustum), r (radius of the smaller end)
records.why: When a cone is cut, the larger end of the frustum is the cone's base, not the 'top'. The bucket (R = top) is the other way up; naming the ends by size avoids contradicting the physical model.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, entries Cone, Conical Frustum, Pyramid, Pyramidal Frustum, Sphere (standard surface-area formulae)

records.old: they must also add the area of the two circular ends (large and small base) to find the total surface area, since the silo is open at the top and closed at the bottom.
records.new: they must also add the area of the closed bottom only (the small circle, πr²), not the open top, to find the surface area to be painted.
records.why: The text said 'open at the top and closed at the bottom' but asked for both circles; the teacher moves and the formative note already (correctly) say only the base is added.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, entries Cone, Conical Frustum, Pyramid, Pyramidal Frustum, Sphere (standard surface-area formulae)
records.group_headline: The Eldoret silo exercise asked for both circular ends although the silo is open at the top; now one circle, with the expected answer added

records.old: (3) In Part D, learners correctly identify that total SA = π(R + r)l + πr² (closed bottom) before Lesson 6.
records.new: (3) In Part D, learners correctly identify that total SA = π(R + r)l + πr² (closed bottom) before Lesson 6. Expected: l = √(2.4² + 0.9²) ≈ 2.56 m; curved area ≈ 16.9 m²; bottom ≈ 1.1 m²; total ≈ 18.0 m².

records.old: both taper from a wider top to a narrower bottom
records.new: both are frustums (a solid with two parallel ends of different sizes): the bucket is wider at the top and the pedestal is wider at the bottom
records.why: The pedestal problem in the next phase has a 30 cm bottom and an 18 cm top, so it is wider at the BOTTOM; the prompt said both are wider at the top.

records.old: 'Njoroge, what is the perpendicular height of your trapezoid — not the slant height, the vertical height inside the trapezoid shape?' → WAIT 13 seconds (this requires Pythagoras or direct measurement — it distinguishes slant height from vertical height and deepens understanding).
records.new: 'Njoroge, what is the perpendicular height of your trapezoid, the distance between its two parallel sides?' → WAIT 13 seconds. Expected: 14 cm. This IS the slant height l of the solid (the trapezoid's height). The vertical height of the whole solid is different: √(14² − 6²) ≈ 12.6 cm, because each top edge sits 6 cm in from the bottom edge.
records.why: The old prompt said the trapezoid's perpendicular height is not the slant height. It is the same length: the lateral face's height is the slant height (14 cm). The solid's own vertical height is √(14² − ((30 − 18)/2)²) = √160 = 12.65 cm, checked twice.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, Pyramidal Frustum (slant height of a lateral face)

records.old: Each learner individually builds a cardboard net of a pyramidal frustum using the dimensions from the Phase 3 trophy stand problem (bottom square 30 cm, top square 18 cm, trapezoidal slant height 14 cm). Guided steps on a task card: '1. Draw and cut out the bottom square base (30 cm × 30 cm). 2. Draw and cut out the top square (18 cm × 18 cm). 3. Draw and cut out four congruent trapezoids (parallel sides 30 cm and 18 cm, slant height 14 cm). 4. Assemble by taping. 5. Lay the net flat and use a ruler to measure the total area of all faces by direct measurement. 6. Compare your measured total to your calculated value of 2244 cm². Record the difference and suggest one reason for any discrepancy.'
records.new: In groups of four, learners build one cardboard net of a pyramidal frustum (manila paper, flip-chart or newspaper sheets are enough; A3 card is just too narrow for a 30 cm square, and each member can cut one or two faces) using the dimensions from the Phase 3 trophy stand problem (bottom square 30 cm, top square 18 cm, trapezoidal slant height 14 cm). Guided steps on a task card: '1. Draw and cut out the bottom square base (30 cm × 30 cm). 2. Draw and cut out the top square (18 cm × 18 cm). 3. Draw and cut out four congruent trapezoids (parallel sides 30 cm and 18 cm, slant height 14 cm). 4. Tape the faces together to check that the solid closes, then lay the faces flat again. 5. Measure each face separately with a ruler and add the measured areas. 6. Compare your measured total to your calculated value of 2244 cm². Record the difference and suggest one reason for any discrepancy.'
records.why: Practical feasibility for a large class with shared scissors: one net per learner of a 30 cm square is too much material and time for the last part of an 80-minute lesson, and A3 (29.7 cm wide) cannot hold a 30 cm square. Step 4 also said to assemble and then 'lay the net flat' in one breath, and step 5 'measure the total area' could simply recompute the formula; measuring each face separately makes it a real check.

records.old: (Compare: conical used π(R+r)l; pyramidal uses 2(a+b)l for lateral area — both are 'slant height × perimeter-related term'.)
records.new: (Compare: conical π(R+r)l = ½ × (sum of the two circumferences) × l; pyramidal 2(a+b)l = ½ × (sum of the two perimeters) × l.) Rectangular-base extension (5 minutes): a frustum with top 18 cm × 10 cm, bottom 36 cm × 20 cm and vertical height 12 cm has two pairs of trapezoids with different slant heights: l₁ = √(12² + 5²) = 13 cm on the 36 cm and 18 cm edges, and l₂ = √(12² + 9²) = 15 cm on the 20 cm and 10 cm edges. TSA (closed) = a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + (a₁ + b₁)l₁ + (a₂ + b₂)l₂ = 180 + 720 + 702 + 450 = 2,052 cm².
records.why: The unit content bullet and the Lesson 7 objective both say 'square or rectangular base', but only the square case was taught or assessed. Worked example recomputed: offsets (20 − 10)/2 = 5 and (36 − 18)/2 = 9; l₁ = √169 = 13, l₂ = √225 = 15; bases 180 + 720 = 900; lateral 54 × 13 = 702 and 30 × 15 = 450; total 2,052. The sides are in ratio 1 : 2 so the top and bottom are similar rectangles, as a true frustum requires.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, Pyramidal Frustum; KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry (surface area of solids)
records.group_headline: Lesson 7 only taught square-based frustums although the sub-strand (and the Lesson 7 objective) says 'square or rectangular'; a short rectangular-base extension with a worked answer is added and the comparison with the cone frustum is sharpened

records.old: For the closing comparison question, cold-call 2 learners and say: 'In one sentence, what is similar between the two frustum lateral area formulas?' → WAIT 12 seconds.
records.new: For the closing comparison question, cold-call 2 learners and say: 'In one sentence, what is similar between the two frustum lateral area formulas?' → WAIT 12 seconds. Then, for the rectangular extension, ask: 'Why can we not just use 2(a + b)l here?' Expected: the two pairs of trapezoids have different slant heights (13 cm and 15 cm), so each pair needs its own term; the total is 2,052 cm².
records.why: Teacher guidance for the new extension.

records.old: For an open-top frustum, the top base area (a²) is omitted.
records.new: For an open-top frustum, the top base area (a²) is omitted. For a frustum with rectangular bases (top a₁ × a₂, bottom b₁ × b₂), TSA = a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + (a₁ + b₁)l₁ + (a₂ + b₂)l₂, where l₁ and l₂ are the slant heights of the two pairs of trapezoids.
records.why: Keeps the Summary Table in step with the rectangular extension.

records.old: the shape you might see in a Maasai granary or a rooftop
records.new: the shape you might see in a planter box, a trophy stand base or a roof
records.why: A Maasai granary is not a typical pyramid frustum; the examples now match Lesson 7's own contexts (planter box, trophy stand).

records.old: (A) Cylinder — radius r = 10.6 cm, height h = 28.4 cm; (B) Open Cone (apex at bottom, open top) — base radius r = 13.4 cm, perpendicular height h = 52.9 cm, slant height l = 54.6 cm; (C) Frustum — top radius R = 14 cm, bottom radius r = 8 cm, slant height l = 26.4 cm, with perpendicular height h = 25.7 cm. Groups calculate the lateral surface area plus base area for each bucket using the formulae established across Lessons 1–7: Cylinder: A = πrl_total = 2πrh + πr²; Cone: A = πrl + πr²; Frustum: A = π(R+r)l + πr² (open top, closed base).
records.new: (A) Cylinder — radius r = 10.6 cm, height h = 28.4 cm; (B) Frustum — top radius R = 14 cm, bottom radius r = 8 cm, slant height l = 26.4 cm, with perpendicular height h = 25.7 cm; (C) Open Cone (apex at bottom, open top) — base radius r = 13.4 cm, perpendicular height h = 52.9 cm, slant height l = 54.6 cm. Groups calculate the sheet metal needed for each open bucket (the Bucket Data Sheet first shown in Lesson 6) using the formulae established across Lessons 1–7: Cylinder: A = 2πrh + πr² (closed base, open top); Frustum: A = π(R+r)l + πr² (open top, closed base); Open cone: A = πrl (curved surface only, because the top is open).
records.why: The cone bucket is open at the top (the data sheet says so) but the formula added a base circle (πr²), giving 2,862 cm² instead of 2,298 cm². Also 'πrl_total' was garbled, and the bucket letters (A cylinder, B cone, C frustum) disagreed with Lesson 1 (A cylinder, B frustum, C cone). Recomputed: cone π(13.4)(54.57) = 2,297 (2,298 with l = 54.6); the three volumes are 10,025, 10,012 and 9,947 cm³, all about 10 litres.
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Mathematics, Strand 2.0 Measurements and Geometry (surface area of solids); Wolfram MathWorld, entries Cone, Conical Frustum, Pyramid, Pyramidal Frustum, Sphere (standard surface-area formulae)
records.group_headline: The conical bucket was costed as if it had a lid although it is open-topped, and the bucket letters (A/B/C) differed between Lessons 1 and 8; every lesson now uses the open cone and Lesson 1's letters

records.old: 'Now calculate the surface area if the frustum also had a lid — how does that change the comparison?'
records.new: 'Now give all three buckets lids. Does the order of the three buckets change?' [Expected: cylinder ≈ 2,597 cm², frustum ≈ 2,641 cm², cone ≈ 2,862 cm², so the frustum is no longer the least.]
records.why: The old extension gave a lid only to the frustum, which makes an unfair comparison. With lids: cylinder 2,244.5 + 353.0 = 2,597; frustum 2,025.1 + π(14²) = 2,641; cone 2,298 + 564 = 2,862. The cone is still the most but the frustum is no longer the least: a real discussion point.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, entries Cone, Conical Frustum, Pyramid, Pyramidal Frustum, Sphere (standard surface-area formulae)

records.new: open cone ≈ π(13.4)(54.6) ≈ 2298 cm² (curved surface only, because the top is open). The cone and cylinder totals differ by only about 2%, so keep l to one decimal place.
records.why: Matches the corrected formulae.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, entries Cone, Conical Frustum, Pyramid, Pyramidal Frustum, Sphere (standard surface-area formulae)

records.old: Under the specific equal-volume dimensions used in this lesson, the open cone required the greatest surface area of sheet metal.
records.new: Under the specific equal-volume dimensions used in this lesson (open cone about 2,298 cm², open cylinder about 2,244 cm², open frustum about 2,025 cm²), the open cone required the greatest surface area of sheet metal and the frustum the least.
records.why: Puts the corrected numbers in the Summary Table.
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, entries Cone, Conical Frustum, Pyramid, Pyramidal Frustum, Sphere (standard surface-area formulae)

records.old: despite potentially higher material costs because their tapered shape makes them easier to stack and carry
records.new: because their tapered shape lets them nest for stacking and makes them easy to carry (and, for our dimensions, they also need the least metal)
records.why: The old sentence said frustum buckets cost more material, which contradicts the lesson's own result (frustum 2,025 cm² is the least of the three).
records.reference: Wolfram MathWorld, entries Cone, Conical Frustum, Pyramid, Pyramidal Frustum, Sphere (standard surface-area formulae)

records.old: (b) No, the claim is not correct for our 10-litre buckets. When the class calculated all three open buckets using the Bucket Data Sheet, the open cone needed the greatest surface area of sheet metal, more than the frustum. So the evidence does not support the claim that the frustum uses the most metal.
records.new: (b) Claim: No, the claim is not correct for our 10-litre buckets. Evidence: when the class calculated all three open buckets using the Bucket Data Sheet, the open cone needed about 2,298 cm², the cylinder about 2,244 cm² and the frustum only about 2,025 cm², so the open cone used the most metal and the frustum the least. Reasoning: surface area depends on the shape's dimensions, not on volume alone; the cone must be very tall to hold 10 litres, so its sloping surface is long. So the evidence does not support the claim that the frustum uses the most metal.
records.why: The exemplar now gives the numbers a marker needs and follows Claim, Evidence, Reasoning.
records.where: Final Explanation, Section 4: Settling the shopkeeper's claim, exemplar

records.old: is the shopkeeper's claim that the frustum bucket uses the most metal correct? Give your reasoning.
records.new: is the shopkeeper's claim that the frustum bucket uses the most metal correct? Answer as Claim (your answer), Evidence (the surface areas you calculated) and Reasoning (the geometry idea that links the evidence to your claim).
records.why: Guideline 7: the summative task should use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with the correct meaning of each part (Claim = answer, Evidence = data, Reasoning = the idea that links them); the unit had no CER at all.
records.where: Final Explanation, Section 4: Settling the shopkeeper's claim, prompt

records.old: Each group nominates a spokesperson to present their sugar-paper findings in a 3-minute 'evidence presentation' to the class.
records.new: Each group nominates a spokesperson, and the teacher selects three groups (including any with different results) to give a 2-minute 'evidence presentation'; the other groups check their sheets against the gallery wall.
records.why: With 8 to 10 groups, 3-minute presentations from every group alone would take 25 to 30 minutes; the lesson then also needs the data-sheet calculation (about 18 min), Evidence Court, writing, the DQB review and 25 minutes of portfolio and model work. Three 2-minute presentations bring the plan to about 80 minutes.
records.group_headline: Lesson 8 planned about 95 minutes of activity for an 80-minute period; whole-class presentations are cut to three 2-minute ones

records.old: Facilitate presentations using a visible 3-minute timer.
records.new: Facilitate the three presentations using a visible 2-minute timer.
records.why: Matches the shortened presentations.

records.old: Collect Portfolio Record Sheets at the end of the lesson. Assess using the KICD rubric indicators: (i) correct solid type identification, (ii) correct formula stated, (iii) correct substitution with units, (iv) correct final answer with units, (v) meaningful real-world interpretation sentence. Learners meeting all five indicators 'Exceed Expectations'. Learners completing (i)–(iv) correctly 'Meet Expectations'.
records.new: Collect Portfolio Record Sheets at the end of the lesson. Suggested dimensions and answers (π = 3.142): (i) conical granary roof, r = 2 m, h = 1.5 m, so l = 2.5 m and curved area ≈ 15.7 m²; (ii) open-top frustum tank, R = 1.8 m, r = 0.9 m, h = 1.2 m, so l = 1.5 m and area = π(2.7)(1.5) + π(0.9²) ≈ 12.7 + 2.5 ≈ 15.3 m²; (iii) spherical tank, r = 1.5 m, area = 4π(1.5²) ≈ 28.3 m²; (iv) square-pyramid roof, base side 8 m, slant height 5 m, area = 4 × ½ × 8 × 5 = 80 m². Assess using the KICD rubric indicators: (i) correct solid type identification, (ii) correct formula stated, (iii) correct substitution with units, (iv) correct final answer with units, (v) meaningful real-world interpretation sentence. Learners meeting all five indicators 'Exceed Expectations'. Learners completing (i)–(iv) correctly 'Meet Expectations'. Learners completing (i)–(iii) 'Approach Expectations'; fewer than three are 'Below Expectations' and need support.
records.why: The portfolio task listed objects but gave no dimensions or answers, so a teacher could not mark it. Suggested values recomputed: 15.71; 12.73 + 2.55 = 15.27; 28.27; 80. The rubric text also only covered Exceed and Meet; Approaches and Below Expectations are added.

records.old: Let us figure out where the formula comes from.'
records.new: Let us figure out where the formula comes from.' Language support: start a two-language word wall (English and Kiswahili) and let learners explain in Kiswahili first if they wish: surface area = eneo la uso; volume = ujazo; circumference = mzingo; diameter = kipenyo; radius = nusu kipenyo; cone = koni; sphere = tufe; cylinder = silinda; pyramid = piramidi; bucket = ndoo.
records.why: Guideline 12 asks for language supports. Teacher decision: these Kiswahili terms are my best knowledge and are not verified against the Kenyan Kiswahili mathematics vocabulary; please confirm or correct them before use, and add terms your learners already use (for example for slant height).
records.group_headline: Added a short English-Kiswahili word wall for the key terms (to be confirmed by a Kiswahili-speaking teacher)

records.old: 'Angalia mifano hii ya ndoo tatu — look at these three bucket shapes.
records.new: 'Angalia ndoo hizi tatu — look at these three buckets.
records.why: Simpler, more natural Kiswahili for 'look at these three buckets'; part of the Kiswahili check above.

value.criterion: Correct use of surface area formulae
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: chooses and states the correct formula for every solid (cone, pyramid, sphere, hemisphere, frustums of cones and pyramids), and correctly distinguishes open from closed shapes and slant height from perpendicular height.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: uses mostly correct formulae with one or two small slips, such as forgetting a base or confusing open and closed.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: uses wrong or missing formulae, or confuses slant height with perpendicular height.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: all calculations are correct and clearly laid out, with correct rounding and units (cm², m²).
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: method is correct but there are minor arithmetic or rounding errors, or a unit is missing.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: method is unclear or contains major errors, and units are missing.

value.criterion: Explaining formulae from nets and derivations
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: clearly explains where πrl, π(R + r)l, 4πr² and 3πr² come from using sectors, annular sectors, cone differences or the orange-peel evidence.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: gives a partly correct explanation of the origin of the formulae, with some steps missing.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: states formulae without explaining where they come from.

value.criterion: Using evidence to judge the shopkeeper's claim (Claim, Evidence, Reasoning)
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: gives a clear Claim, uses the Lesson 8 numbers as Evidence, links them with Reasoning about the dimensions, and explains that equal volume does not mean equal surface area without overgeneralising.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: reaches the correct Claim but gives limited Evidence or does not note that the result depends on the dimensions.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: accepts or rejects the claim without evidence from calculation.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: links the mathematics to real Kenyan uses (buckets, tanks, silos, tents) and gives sensible reasons why shape choice balances cost, stacking and strength.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: gives a Kenyan example with a simple reason.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: gives no real-life link or an irrelevant one.

records.why: The contract has only three level fields, so each descriptor now names its CBE level (Exceeds / Meets / Approaches Expectations) in the text. The 'Claim, Evidence, Reasoning' wording is added to criterion 4 to match the new Section 4(b) prompt, and frustums of pyramids are added to criterion 1 because Section 3 now assesses them.
